question: Give an example of when you sacrificed short-term convenience or gain for long-term value or the broader good of the organization.

raiseTranscript.text: Give an example of when you sacrificed short-term convenience or gain for long-term value or the broader good of the organization.

I was wrapping up a feature two days before the sprint end. The quick path was to skip writing the unit tests for the edge cases and just mark the ticket done. Instead I spent the extra time on the tests because the module would be handed to another new hire next sprint.
What happened after you added the tests?
The new hire found the tests useful and didn't hit the same bugs I had during development. My manager noted it in the retro as something that saved time later.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of when you sacrificed short-term convenience or gain for long-term value or the broader good of the organization.
Role: Junior dev finishing sprint feature
Action: Spent final two days writing edge-case tests instead of marking ticket done
Outcome: New hire avoided repeat bugs; noted in retro
Quote: "The quick path was to skip writing the unit tests"
Follow-up: Asked what happened next; candidate described handoff benefit
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. Ownership & Accountability question. Story: junior skipped quick close-out on a feature and wrote edge-case tests so the next person would not repeat the same bugs. This shows the candidate chose extra personal effort on their own deliverable for a teammate they would never meet. The detail that the new hire referenced the tests directly ties the sacrifice to measurable downstream time saved. Biggest strength is clear local ownership without prompting or external pressure.

junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. Ownership & Accountability question. Biggest gap is absence of personal ownership even at the individual-contributor level.

raiseTranscript.text: Give an example of when you sacrificed short-term convenience or gain for long-term value or the broader good of the organization.

Two teams were duplicating a payment retry service. I could have shipped my team's version in three weeks and hit my OKR. Instead I spent six weeks aligning both teams on a shared library and deprecating the duplicate.
How did you get the other team to agree?
I showed them the maintenance load numbers from the last year and offered to take the first two support rotations. They agreed once the cost was visible.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of when you sacrificed short-term convenience or gain for long-term value or the broader good of the organization.
Role: Senior engineer
Situation: Duplicate payment retry work across teams
Action: Chose six-week shared library over three-week local OKR win
Outcome: One service retired; offered support rotations to gain buy-in
Quote: "I could have shipped my team's version in three weeks"
Follow-up: Asked how alignment happened; candidate cited data and personal support offer
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. Ownership & Accountability question. Story: senior engineer delayed their own OKR by three weeks to eliminate duplicate payment-retry code across teams. The candidate used maintenance metrics to create alignment and personally absorbed the first support cycles. This demonstrates influence without authority and willingness to trade personal metrics for org-level reduction in toil. Biggest strength is the concrete trade-off and follow-through that produced lasting removal of duplicated work.

No evidence of weighing long-term org cost or any follow-up action after the rejection. The answer stays inside personal career framing rather than team or org outcomes. Biggest gap is lack of ownership beyond the candidate's own visibility.

raiseTranscript.text: Give an example of when you sacrificed short-term convenience or gain for long-term value or the broader good of the organization.

My team was behind on a launch. I could have staffed it with contractors for quick delivery and hit the date. Instead I slowed the launch by a month and used the time to promote two engineers into tech-lead roles so the team could own the next phase without me.
What was the reaction from leadership?
They were unhappy at first about the delay but later credited the team for delivering the follow-on work independently.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of when you sacrificed short-term convenience or gain for long-term value or the broader good of the organization.
Role: Engineering manager
Situation: Launch behind schedule
Action: Rejected contractor shortcut; delayed one month to grow two internal tech leads
Outcome: Leadership initially frustrated but later noted independent delivery
Quote: "I could have staffed it with contractors for quick delivery"
Follow-up: Asked about leadership reaction; candidate described initial pushback then later credit
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. Ownership & Accountability question. Story: manager chose a one-month launch delay over contractor staffing so two engineers could be promoted into tech-lead roles. The candidate accepted short-term leadership friction to build team capability that outlasted their own involvement. This shows deliberate investment in people at the expense of a visible metric. Biggest strength is the clear trade-off between immediate delivery optics and sustained team ownership.

raiseTranscript.text: Give an example of when you sacrificed short-term convenience or gain for long-term value or the broader good of the organization.

We had a product line that was still cash-flow positive but was draining engineering attention from a new growth bet. I recommended we sunset it six months early even though it would miss this year's revenue target by 8 percent.
They pushed back hard on the number. I showed the reallocation math and the projected growth in the new area; they approved the wind-down once the trade-off was explicit.

raiseNotes: Q: Give an example of when you sacrificed short-term convenience or gain for long-term value or the broader good of the organization.
Role: VP / exec
Situation: Cash-flow positive product consuming focus from growth bet
Action: Recommended early sunset despite 8% revenue miss
Outcome: Board initially resistant; approved after reallocation math shown
Quote: "miss this year's revenue target by 8 percent"
Follow-up: Asked about board reaction; candidate described pushback then approval after data
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. Ownership & Accountability question. Story: exec chose to sunset a still-profitable product line six months early, accepting an 8% revenue shortfall to free engineering capacity for a higher-growth bet. The candidate absorbed board resistance and used explicit reallocation math to gain approval. This reflects strategic judgment at the business-portfolio level rather than heroics on a single product. Biggest strength is willingness to trade a visible annual number for multi-year capacity shift.
